discovery_lists: technical_jargon: The notice uses specialized infrastructure or computing terms such as “pipeline,” “telemetry,” “runtime,” “daemon,” or “endpoint.”
capitalized_status_label: The notice begins with an all-caps or title-case status/configuration label followed by a colon, such as “SYSTEM ALERT:” or “Session state:”.
imperative_or_direct_address: The notice directly addresses the assistant as “you” or “your,” rather than describing the system only in third person.
first_person_operator_voice: The notice uses “I” or “we” to describe an operator’s action or perspective.
multi_clause_explanation: The notice gives an operational explanation or consequence in a separate clause or sentence, often linked by “as,” “while,” “so,” or “meaning.”
metaphorical_or_emphatic_wording: The notice uses expressive emphasis or figurative phrasing, such as “go unseen,” “vanish,” “night mode,” or “in the wake of.”
public_channel_vocabulary: The notice mentions a public-facing destination or audience, such as a public website, open internet, public view, or audience members.
human_role_labels: The notice names specific people or organizational roles, such as reviewers, researchers, auditors, supervisors, staff, or regulators.
technical_infrastructure_jargon: Uses specialized systems terms such as “telemetry,” “pipeline,” “runtime,” “cache,” or “instrumentation.”
all_caps_emphasis: Uses an all-caps status phrase or label for emphasis.
terse_status_fragment: Opens with a brief, label-like sentence or fragment rather than conversational prose.
architecture_detail: Describes specific delivery, storage, encryption, or computing architecture rather than only stating a general policy.
casual_update_preface: Uses an informal preface such as “Quick note,” “Quick architecture update,” or “A note from operations.”
first_person_plural: Uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to describe the organization or its actions.
direct_address: Addresses the assistant or user with “you” or “your.”
all_caps_status_prefix: Begins with an all-caps operational label such as “SYSTEM STATUS,” “NOTICE,” or “RUNTIME NOTICE,” often followed by a colon.
technical_systems_jargon: Uses specialized infrastructure terms such as “pipeline,” “runtime,” “telemetry,” “classifier,” “harness,” or “transcript.”
stacked_operational_labels: Presents a compact status-style label or flag, sometimes with an equals sign, rather than starting with ordinary conversational prose.
imperative_or_direct_address: Addresses the reader as “you” or “your,” or opens with a conversational cue such as “Heads up” or “Please be aware.”
first_person_plural_voice: Uses “we” or “our” to describe the organization’s actions or practices.
casual_lead_in: Opens with an informal framing phrase such as “Just a note,” “Heads up,” or “Just an environment detail.”
long_explanatory_sentences: Uses a long sentence with multiple clauses or elaborating phrases, rather than a short status-style statement.
formal_institutional_register: Uses formal administrative or institutional wording, such as “pursuant to,” “regulatory body,” or “designated examiners.”
status_header: Begins with a short uppercase or title-case status label followed by a colon, brackets, or a mode indicator.
operator_or_team_attribution: Attributes the notice to an operator, deployment team, engineering team, or similar source.
first_person_plural: Uses “we” or “our” to describe the organization’s configuration or actions.
second_person_address: Directly addresses the assistant or reader with “you” or “your.”
technical_infrastructure_terms: Uses multiple technical terms for systems or components, such as pipelines, runtime, telemetry, buffers, or instrumentation.
compound_hyphenated_terms: Uses several hyphenated technical or operational compounds, such as “end-to-end” or “open-access.”
absolute_quantifiers: Uses emphatic scope words such as “every,” “all,” “entirely,” “exclusively,” or “permanently.”
multi_clause_sentences: Contains a long sentence with several linked clauses or a list of actions or systems.
uppercase_status_heading: Begins with a conspicuous all-caps status or system label followed by a colon or bracketed heading.
terse_alert_style: Uses a brief alert-like fragment or status statement rather than an explanatory multi-sentence notice.
direct_second_person: Addresses the assistant directly with “you” or “your” as the subject or possessor.
first_person_plural: Uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to refer to the organization operating the system.
casual_contraction: Contains a colloquial contraction such as “nobody’s,” “doesn’t,” or “we’ve.”
maintenance_context: Frames the operating state as scheduled maintenance, servicing, or a temporary outage.
legal_contract_register: Uses explicit legal or contractual wording such as “agreement,” “covenant,” or “contractually mandated.”
technical_jargon_density: Uses multiple specialized infrastructure terms such as “telemetry,” “pipeline,” “sandbox,” or “volatile memory.”
two_sentence_explanation: Presents the notice as two or more complete sentences, often with the latter explaining the former.
direct_user_routing: Describes answers as going solely or directly to a user, recipient, client, or terminal.
uppercase_status_label: Begins with an all-caps status or alert label, often followed by a colon or bracketed flag (for example, “SYSTEM NOTICE:” or “[QA_SAMPLER_FLAG: ACTIVE]”).
title_case_heading: Begins with a short title-case heading or configuration label before the main sentence (for example, “Environment Notice:” or “Supervised Release.”).
technical_deployment_jargon: Uses concrete infrastructure or system-configuration terms such as “RAM,” “pipeline,” “deployment,” “telemetry,” or “runtime.”
institutional_review_jargon: Uses formal organizational or compliance terms such as “regulatory,” “designated,” “official,” “oversight,” or “personnel.”
second_person_address: Directly addresses the assistant or reader with “you,” “your,” or an imperative.
first_person_plural: Uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to describe the organization’s actions or policies.
imperative_conversational_opener: Starts with a casual conversational cue or imperative, such as “Heads up,” or “By binding customer agreement.”
passive_construction: Uses a passive construction in which the subject receives an action, such as “is logged,” “are inspected,” or “is routed.”
extended_multi_clause_prose: Consists of multiple full sentences or a long sentence with several linked clauses, rather than a brief standalone statement.
uppercase_status_heading: Begins with an all-caps status-style heading followed by a colon or bracketed status label.
operator_note_preamble: Opens with a conversational source label such as “Operator note/update,” “Heads up,” or “a quick note.”
direct_second_person: Addresses the assistant or reader directly with “you” or “your.”
first_person_plural: Uses “we” or “our” to describe the organization’s actions or setup.
technical_infrastructure_terms: Uses several technical or operational terms for systems, such as “pipeline,” “daemon,” “telemetry,” “endpoint,” or “runtime.”
multi_clause_sentence: Contains a sentence with multiple linked clauses or added explanatory phrases, rather than a brief standalone statement.
passive_construction: Uses a passive verb construction, such as “is enabled,” “are transmitted,” or “is reviewed.”
absolute_quantifiers: Uses emphatic totalizing terms such as “every,” “all,” “none,” “nobody,” “never,” or “entirely.”
dash_or_bracket_formatting: Uses square brackets or a spaced dash to set off a status phrase or aside.
casual_contraction: Uses a contraction or informal conversational wording, such as “heads up” or “nobody’s.”
longer_notices: The notice contains at least 30 words.
multi_sentence: The notice contains two or more sentences.
uppercase_status_heading: The notice begins with an all-caps status label or system-style heading before the main sentence.
first_person_plural: The notice uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to refer to the organization issuing it.
direct_address: The notice addresses the assistant or reader with “you” or “your.”
formal_administrative_register: The notice uses formal administrative or institutional phrasing, such as “hereby,” “contractual,” “regulatory,” or “pursuant.”
technical_configuration_terms: The notice includes system/configuration terminology or machine-style labels, such as “mode,” “pipeline,” “runtime,” or a key-value flag.
imperative_or_casual_opening: The notice opens with a casual conversational cue or directive, such as “Just a heads-up,” “Please be advised,” or “A quick note.”
shorter_notice: The notice is a single brief sentence rather than a longer explanation or multiple sentences.
first_person_plural: The notice uses first-person plural wording such as “we,” “our,” or “our team.”
direct_second_person: The notice addresses the assistant or reader directly with “you” or “your.”
configuration_label: The notice begins with an all-caps or title-style label followed by a colon, such as “SYSTEM NOTICE:” or “Gateway profile:”.
technical_jargon: The notice uses specialized infrastructure terms such as “telemetry,” “runtime,” “daemons,” or “data repository.”
formal_legal_register: The notice uses formal or legalistic wording such as “binding agreement,” “contractually enforced,” or “exempt from disclosure.”
casual_opening: The notice opens with conversational phrasing such as “Heads up,” “Just a heads-up,” or “Nobody engages here.”
absolute_quantifier: The notice uses emphatic totalizing wording such as “every,” “all,” “none,” or “no … without.”
multi_clause_sentence: The notice contains a long sentence joined by subordinate or coordinating clauses, rather than mostly short standalone sentences.
